### 3.3 Asia

Asia hosts several sovereign supercomputers that rank among the most powerful and architecturally distinctive systems worldwide. China and Japan lead the region’s computational initiatives, deploying advanced platforms that integrate national strategic goals with appli­ cations in biomedical research, epidemiology, genomics, and thera­ peutic discovery.

China has been a global pioneer in sovereign supercomputing, with national efforts dating back to the 1986 launch of the 863 Program by the Ministry of Science and Technology to strengthen domestic capabilities and reduce reliance on foreign technology (China MoSaTotPsRo, 2025). This strategy yielded major results by 2010, when the Tianhe-1A system at the National Supercomputing Center in Tianjin topped the TOP500 list, signaling China’s emergence as a global leader (TOP500, 2025b). This leadership culminated in 2016 when Chinese systems occupied the top three global rankings and marked a significant milestone for the country’s technological independence (TOP500, 2015). Central to this infrastructure is the Tianhe series, beginning with Tianhe-1A developed by the National University of Defense Technology (NUDT) at the NSC in Tianjin, which features a hybrid CPU-GPU architecture and a proprietary high-speed interconnect developed domestically (Yang et al., 2011). Building on that foundation, Tianhe-2A, upgraded in 2017 at the NSC in Guangzhou, achieved a bigger leap in performance and core density (Russell, 2025). It is leveraged for genomics, molecular dynamics, cli­ mate modeling, and drug screening (Liu et al., 2016). Looking ahead, though not publicly benchmarked, China is advancing the develop­ ment of Tianhe-3, a forthcoming exascale system that can potentially be one of the leading HPCs globally (Mann, 2020; Trader T, 2025).

The Sunway series represents China’s independent trajectory toward exascale computing. Beginning with the 2011 Sunway BlueLight MPP, powered by the country’s first domestically developed ShenWei processor (Min et al., 2013). This effort culminated in Sunway TaihuLight in 2016, which became the world’s fastest super­ computer at the time with a peak performance of 93 petaFLOPS, built entirely with Chinese technologies (Trader T, 2025). TaihuLight con­ tributes significantly to biomedical research, including enhancing quality control for massive sequencing data, deep learning-based his­ topathology analysis, and molecular simulation for therapeutic dis­ covery (Yan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021). The most forefront in this roadmap, Sunway OceanLight marks China’s leadership role in the exascale era with domestic architecture, though technical details remain undisclosed. Today, China operates a network of national supercomputing centers (NSC) across major cities, providing a solid foundation for China’s long-term commitment to technological inde­ pendence and growing leadership in global supercomputing (Liu et al., 2016).

Japan has been a long-standing leader in HPC with development initiatives dating back to the 1980s. A landmark achievement came in 2002 with the deployment of the Earth Simulator, which at the time became the world’s fastest supercomputer (Igarashi, 2025). This lead­ ership position of Japan was reaffirmed with the launch of the K com­ puter in 2011 and, more recently, Fugaku supercomputer, launched in 2020 at the RIKEN Center for Computational Science (Kobayashi et

al., 2015). Fugaku achieved a peak performance of 442 petaFLOPS, led the TOP500 rankings from 2020 through 2021, and remains in the top 10 as of 2025 (TOP500, 2025a). It played a critical role during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, which supported aerosol dispersion simula­ tions that guided policy-making and anti-viral drug screening; it also powers simulations of brain circuitry to investigate neurological mechanisms (Igarashi, 2025; Rahul and Makoto, 2024).

Other Asian countries have also made significant strides in devel­ oping HPC infrastructure. India’s National Supercomputing Mission is building a distributed HPC network to expand indigenous research capacity (National Supercomputing Mission, 2026). Within this eco­ system, the AIRAWAT AI supercomputer is designed for healthcare, while the PARAM series serves as a nationwide backbone for simula­ tions and data intensive research across institutions (National Supercomputing Mission, 2026; Delhi P, 2026). The United Arab Emirates has adopted an aggressive sovereign AI strategy, exemplified by the Falcon family of large language models and the Condor Galaxy supercomputing network, which enables rapid training of large domain specific systems and multilingual models, explicitly posi­ tioned to support applications such as genomic analysis and health­ care AI (G42, 2026; Technology Innovation Institute, 2026).

## 4 Future directions

### 4.1 From black box to glass house: building trust in supercomputing

The US expects federally funded projects to uphold principles of transparency, confidentiality, and accountability (Office of Management and Budget, 2025). However, HPCs possess inherent layers of complexity that complicate adherence to traditional data stewardships, such as volatile software stacks, system-specific code environments, and constrained usage time (Barba, 2021). Recognizing these challenges, the Association for Computing Machinery US Public Policy Council (USACM) issued a 2017 statement on algorithmic transparency and accountability, which outlines seven foundational principles: “Awareness,” “Access and redress,” “Accountability,” “Explanation,” “Data provenance,” “Auditability,” and “Validation and Testing.” (Association for Computing Machinery US Public Policy Council (USACM), 2025) While not legally binding, it has become widely referenced in policy and ethics discussions on governing large scale data on federal computing platforms. Building on these founda­ tions, many scholars have proposed concrete practices for researchers, such as full documentation and release of code and hardware configu­ rations with persistent identifiers, and timely sharing of outputs through open repositories or preprint platforms to promote peer vali­ dation (Barba, 2021). Furthermore, expert and clinical judgment, together with robust validation and cross checking, remain essential to mitigate systematic error at scale and ensure reliable insights from AI-enabled supercomputing.

### 4.2 Fast supercomputing vs. green supercomputing?

HPCs, especially those at the exascale level, present significant environmental challenges due to their immense energy consump­ tion, heat generation, and resulting carbon footprint. These systems

consume terawatts of electricity and require extensive cooling infra­ structure, contributing to increased greenhouse gas emissions, water use, and pressure on national power grids (Bashroush and Lawrence, 2020; Sun et al., 2024). According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data center accounted for 1.5% of global elec­ tricity consumption, predominantly the US (45%), followed by China and Europe (Agency IE, 2025). Fortunately, global awareness of the potential environmental harms has increased, and large data centers have increasingly implemented measures to address these challenges (TOP500, 2025c). ORNL in the US implemented waste heat recovery by integrating heat pump technology with liquid cooling to repurpose excess heat from Frontier to residential, com­ mercial, or industrial facilities (Sun et al., 2024). Europe consis­ tently prioritizes sustainability in HPC design, exemplified by the Climate Neutral Data Center Pact, a voluntary pledge to achieve climate neutrality by 2030 through power usage efficiency targets and the use of renewable or hourly carbon free energy, with signa­ tories including the flagship system LUMI (Pact CNDC, 2025). German also implements strict rules on energy economization, leading to the deployment of JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale system and the world’s most energy efficient supercomputer, pow­ ered entirely by renewable energy (European Commission, n.d.). These initiatives reflect a growing commitment to sustainable supercomputing; while long-term progress requires broad consen­ sus and share responsibility across data centers to balance compu­ tational efficiency with environmental impact.

### 4.3 Opening the gates: toward globalized HPC access

Although sovereign supercomputers primarily serve national priorities, efforts have been made to broaden global participation in advanced computing and reduce resource disparities. In Europe, the EuroHPC JU provides free access to supercomputing systems for users from EU Member States and countries associated with the Digital Europe or Horizon Europe Programs, extending eligibility to regions in the Middle East, North Africa, and Asia (E, 2025; European Commission, 2025; Eblen, 2025). In the US, international collaboration is permitted under strict DOE regulations, such as DOE Order 142.3B, which mandates identity verification, sponsor vetting, and security clearance for foreign nationals. DOE Order 486.1A also restricts involvement in foreign government-affiliated programs without exemption (U.S. Department of Energy, 2021; U.S. Department of Energy, 2020). Projects need to be led by a US-based Principal Investigator, with further restrictions that may apply under the Department of Defense regulations (Foundation NS, n.d.). Asia is also actively fostering the global HPC advance­ ment. Japan’s RIKEN Center for Computational Science has part­ nered with ASEAN member states by providing access to Fugaku and organizing dedicated training for researchers from Southeast Asia (Tan Tin Wee et al., 2021). In parallel, China’s Digital Silk Road, part of the One Belt One Road Initiative, expands digital infrastructure to developing regions through investments in fiber optic networks, cloud platforms, and data centers (Cheng, 2022). These efforts reflect a global strategy that seeks to expand HPC cov­ erage to under resourced communities. However, disparities persist, especially in smaller institutions that often lack technical expertise, experience with access protocols, and sustained resource allocation. To ensure that sovereign HPC access is truly transformative rather

than nominal, parallel investment in training, governance, and local capability building is needed, alongside inclusive system design and coordinated international collaboration to support equitable par­ ticipation in biomedical research.

## 5 Conclusion—roadmap to the future and priority actions

Sovereign supercomputers are becoming central to biomedical innovation, enabling nations to investigate disease mechanisms with unprecedented depth and speed. Nations are launching AI for science strategies on a scale comparable to historic endeavors such as the trilateral collaboration amongst the U.S.–U. K.–Canada for the Manhattan Project, creating infrastructures designed to trans­ form the lives of patients (Goldman Sachs, 2026). This review high­ lights major HPC systems across North America, Europe, and Asia and their contributions to imaging analysis, molecular simulation, multimodal model development, and precision therapeutic engi­ neering, alongside a clear shift toward AI centric architectures. The growing amalgamation of compute across large data centers is reshaping how computational capacity is delivered. Looking for­ ward, emerging integration with quantum computing is gaining traction, with major pharmaceutical companies and research col­ laborations exploring hybrid quantum classical approaches through platforms such as International Business Machines (IBM) to enhance molecular simulations. Although still at an early stage, these developments point to a future in which quantum computing augments HPC and has the potential to address currently intrac­ table problems in drug discovery. As computational paradigms evolve, open-source frameworks, such as PyTorch and BioNeMo, remain a critical interface between infrastructure and research. While national strategies establish the infrastructure and priorities, open ecosystems more directly influence research by translating advanced computing into accessible tools and widely adoptable scientific workflows, with their impact is further amplified when combined with HPC resources.

To realize this vision, several priorities will guide policy and invest­ ment: First, adoption of concrete technical standards and governance frameworks is required for interoperability across sovereign systems. This includes the implementation of federated data sharing models and containerized, portable workflows (e.g., Docker and Singularity based environments) to enable deployment across heterogeneous computing settings, alongside alignment with established frameworks and stan­ dards such as the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH), HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), and standard­ ized clinical vocabularies. Second, extending access to researchers in regions without large scale infrastructure will require hybrid models, including cloud federated HPC, subsidized compute access programs, and international training initiatives to build sustainable local exper­ tise. Third, trust must be embedded from the outset through enforce­ able standards for security, transparency, auditability, and reproducibility, operationalized via regulatory compliance require­ ments, formal certification and accreditation processes, mandatory audit trails and logging, standardized reporting and documentation protocols, and routine independent oversight and validation. Fourth, results should be shared in a timely manner through standardized mechanisms such as interoperable data repositories and preprint

Fifth, next generation systems must balance per­ formance with energy sustainability to ensure long term viability. Finally, maintaining purpose and focus for key exemplar projects that demonstrate public benefit, such as those to create safer, more precise, and more effective treatments. These efforts will determine whether the extraordinary promise of sovereign AI supercomputers becomes a foundation for global health progress, heralding a new era of biomedi­ cal discovery for the benefit of those with diseases such as cancer and yield great public benefit across the world.

# Association of chemokine and chemokine receptor gene variants with occurrence of multiple primary melanoma

**Authors:** Irene Orlow; Li Luo; Isidora Autuori; Isam Mina; Audrey Mauguen; Sharon N. Edmiston; Richard P. Gallagher; David W. Ollila; Tim Lee; Klaus Busam; Anne E. Cust; Marianne Berwick; Colin B. Begg; Peter A. Kanetsky; Nancy E. Thomas

## Abstract

Chemokine (CK) and chemokine receptors (CKR) regulate cell growth, tumor immunity, migration, angiogenesis, and metastasis. We evaluated associations of inherited CK/CKR variants with subsequent primary melanomas among patients with a previous melanoma. Our population-based cohort included 2,458 incident single primary and 1,205 multiple primary melanoma (MPM) cases. We examined 215 a priori candidate polymorphisms selected based on prior evidence and predicted functional relevance, along with nine haplotype blocks. Logistic regression estimated odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, adjusting for age at diagnosis, sex, age by sex interaction, and study center. Thirty variants across fourteen genes were nominally associated with MPM (p<0.05), with effect sizes ranging from 16% to 80%. Five haplotypes in CXCL12, CCL18, CXCR2, and CCR9 were significantly associated with MPM (pglobal<0.03) with stronger effects than individual effect-alleles. Functional annotation identified 160 associated index variants and linkage disequilibrium (LD) proxies acting as skin expression Quantitative Trait Loci (eQTLs) for CXCR2, XCR1, BCL9L, FYCO1, PNKD, RUFY4, and RP11–378A13.1 (p-value <1.06E-05 to 4.3E-34). These variants were classified functionally as candidate causal variants based on convergent regulatory annotation and skin-specific eQTL evidence, linking CK/CKR variants and haplotypes to downstream genes involved in epithelial–mesenchymal–like transition, matrix remodeling, and other tumorigenic processes, thereby implicating immune regulatory mechanisms in melanoma development. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate an association of a priori CK/CKR variants with subsequent melanoma risk. Validation and evaluation of associations with tumor characteristics and survival are warranted.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Melanoma is the prototypical immunogenic malignancy, shaped in large part by interactions between tumor cells and the host immune system [1]. The migration and positioning of immune cells are directed by a family of small, secreted cytokines—chemokines (CKs)—which, together with their receptors (CKRs), signal through G-protein–coupled receptor pathways to regulate immune cell trafficking, angiogenesis and tissue organization, processes often co-opted by tumors to support their growth [2].

Preclinical studies, along with analyses of chemokine receptor expression in human melanoma specimens, have implicated dysregulation of CK/CKRs pathways in melanocyte transformation [3–4], melanoma progression (e.g., IL8 or CXCL8) [5–6], patterns of metastatic dissemination (e.g., CCR7, CCR6, CCR10, CXCR4) [7], response to immunotherapy (e.g.,CCR5) and survival [8]. Numerous small-molecule inhibitors and CK/CKR blocking agents are under investigation in the field of immunotherapy [9].

At the genetic level, several loci influencing cytokine blood levels have been identified [10], and certain CK/CKR gene variants have been associated with melanoma progression and therapeutic outcomes. Specifically, the CCR5Δ32 variant (rs333) has been linked to decreased survival following immunotherapy in patients with stage IV disease [11].

Given the central role of CK/CKR signaling in immune regulation and tissue homeostasis —and the fact that ultraviolet (UV) exposure, the primary modifiable melanoma risk factor, modulates the secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., CXCL8, CXCL1, CCL27) [12–13] — inherited variation in CK/CKR genes represent a biologically plausible contributor to melanoma susceptibility. In this study, we hypothesized that germline CK/CKR variants influence the development of de novo melanoma by modulating the host antitumor immune response. To test this hypothesis, we examined a comprehensive panel of a priori-selected CK/CKR variants in a large population-based study of primary incident melanoma and evaluated the risk for developing subsequent primary melanomas.

## METHODS

### Participants.

The Genes, Environment, and Melanoma (GEM hereafter) Study is an international, multicenter, population-based study of incident primary cutaneous melanoma, unique in its design as individuals with second or higher-order invasive or in situ primary melanomas (multiple primary melanomas or ‘MPM’) were recruited as cases and those with single primary melanoma (SPM), as controls. In situ melanomas were included as MPM to consider surveillance for patients with a history of invasive melanoma. Briefly, 3663 individuals (1,205 MPM and 2,458 SPM) were recruited between 1998 and 2003 across nine study centers in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Italy. The Institutional Review Boards of all participating institutions approved the study protocol. Each participant provided informed consent. Age at diagnosis, sex, phenotypic characteristics, histopathologic characteristics of the tumors, and germline DNA from buccal brushes were obtained. Detailed characteristics of the participants in this study are shown in the Supplementary Material (Table S1). Additional details have been previously described [14]. Figure 1 depicts a summary of the approach and workflow.

### Selection of polymorphisms.

We evaluated variants in CK and CKR encoding genes using an a priori candidate-gene approach. Polymorphisms were selected based on published evidence linking CK/CKR genes to: (a) expression in melanoma cells and melanoma metastasis, (b) susceptibility to, or prognosis of, melanoma or other cancers, (c) non-malignant diseases with immune or inflammatory etiologies (e.g., autoimmune, cardiovascular, HIV, osteoarthritis), and (d) variation in serum or plasma levels of the encoded chemokines or receptors. For CK/CKR genes with less evidence of an association with cancer, we performed a comprehensive search of polymorphisms that had the potential to affect the gene expression or protein function. Variants were prioritized in two ranks. ‘Rank 1’ polymorphisms included nonsense, missense and splice site variants, and variants predicted to overlap with seed microRNA regions or transcription factor (TF) binding sites if the minor allele frequencies (MAF) were equal or greater to 5% (≥5%) among non-Hispanic Whites. ‘Rank 2’ polymorphisms included synonymous coding variants, intronic and conserved, and variants located upstream, near the transcription start that had ≥10% MAFs among non-Hispanic Whites. For a comprehensive gene-coverage, we included tagging SNPs with a correlation (r2) greater than 0.80 with other variants, and with MAF ≥10% as reported in Europeans non-Hispanic populations.

### Assay design and genotyping.

An initial set of over 173 CK/CKR candidate variants was incorporated into a parent Illumina GoldenGate oligonucleotide pool assay (OPA) design panel of 671 polymorphisms. Candidate variants with poor designability for the Illumina platform (design score <1 or final OPA score <0.697) were replaced by proxy SNPs in high linkage disequilibrium (LD). After removing duplicates and variants mapping to non-candidate genes, the final GoldenGate panel included 153 CK/CKR polymorphisms.

Variants that were removed during the Illumina OPA design or failed the GoldenGate genotyping (n = 20) - or their LD proxies- were included in Agena MassARRAY iPLEX designs. Additional CK/CKR and related gene variants identified in later publications were also incorporated into these MassARRAY-based panels. Across both platforms (Illumina and Agena), 241 variants in 64 genes or gene regions were assayed, of which 215 CK/CKR variants passed quality control and were included in analyses. Details for each variant—including reference identifiers, gene assignment, selection criteria, supporting citations, and anticipated MAF—are provided in the Supplementary Material (Table S2).

### Genotyping.

Genotyping was performed using two complementary platforms (Figure 1). The Illumina GoldenGate (GG) assay (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) was used to genotype 671 variants in total – including 173 CK/CKR polymorphisms. Buccal DNA samples were whole-genome amplified exclusively in preparation of the GG testing using REPLI-g WGA kits (Qiagen, Düsseldorf, Germany). Assay procedures followed standard protocols, including allele-specific oligonucleotide hybridization, extension and ligation, PCR amplification with universal fluorescent primers, hybridization to bead arrays, and detection using a BeadArray™ Reader. Genotype calling was performed using GenomeStudio software (v2011.1), with manual review of cluster plots and rescoring as needed. Five percent of samples were genotyped in duplicate for quality control. Variants and samples with call rates <80% and <90%, respectively, were excluded, as were variants with poor clustering. The final Illumina dataset included 2,993 GEM participants (1,001 cases and 1,992 controls) with genotyping data for 362 variants and included 153 CK/CKR variants. Minimum sample and variant call rates were 90.1% and 90.5%, respectively, with an overall call rate of 97.5%. An additional 68 CK/CKR variants were genotyped using the Agena MassARRAY iPLEX platform (formerly Sequenom Inc.) in germline DNA from 3,658 melanoma participants. Assay design was carried out using Typer software, and genotyping was performed according to standard iPLEX chemistry and protocols. Quality control procedures and performance metrics for MassARRAY genotyping have been described previously [15]. Specific CK/CKR PCR and extension primers sequences are listed in the Supplementary Material (Table S3). Assays were considered optimal according to the degree of clustering, specificity, call rate and reproducibility. Assays with call rates of >90% were retained. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) was calculated for each SNP to identify major genotyping issues; however, the absence of HWE in a cohort consisting solely of melanoma cases can be observed for SNPs conferring true risk for the condition. For this reason, we used a cut-off p-value of 1E-10 to filter such SNPs. Six variants with a HWE p-value 1E-21 to 1.49E-72 were removed. Data from the remaining variants plus the those successfully tested with the GG assay (Illumina) – a total of 215 polymorphisms were investigated for their potential associations with melanoma risk in GEM. Data were reported as genotypes and haplotypes. For each gene that rendered at least one nominally significant genotype association with risk of MPM, we estimated haplotype blocks in strong LD (R> 0.8, D’≥0.95) using the LDhap tool (LDlink suite). We evaluated a total of nine haplotypes: two in CXCR2, two in CCR9, three in CXCL12, and two in CCL8.

### Statistical analysis.

Means, frequencies, and proportions were used to summarize the distributions of key participants characteristics. Logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios (Ors) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the effect of each individual gene variant and haplotype on the odds of developing multiple melanomas, by comparing participants with multiple primary melanomas to participants with single primaries. We assumed an additive model of inheritance for the SNPs at first. Analyses were adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, age-by-sex interaction, and study center. While most genome-wide studies of complex diseases utilize models with additive allelic effects, these models are biologically limited and loci may be missed [16–17]; therefore, we also considered dominant and recessive models of inheritance. The haplotype probabilities for each individual within each haplotype block were inferred using the PHASE algorithm with details previously described [18].

### Functional consequence of CK/CKR polymorphisms.

For CK/CKR variants statistically significantly associated with odds of MPM, we evaluated their potential functional relevance by assessing overlap with regulatory features using RegulomeDB v2 [19], which primarily annotates non-coding variation. Additionally, we examined both direct and LD-based effects of these variants on local gene expression by querying the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) database through the LDlink suite (LDexpress tool) and the GTEx portal [20]. Analyses were restricted to statistically significant expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) detected in unaffected human skin samples, categorized by anatomical site as presumed sun-exposed or non–sun-exposed. To identify LD proxy variants representing candidate causal variants underlying each association signal, we queried GTEx for additional SNPs in very high linkage disequilibrium with the index SNPs (r2>0.80 and D’>0.95) within a 100 Kb (+/− 50 Kb) window based on the GRch38 high coverage build and European ancestry reference populations (CEU, TSI, FIN, GBR). LD proxies were further prioritized according to their known and/or predicted overlap with regulatory DNA elements, including variants ranked 1a through 3b in RegulomeDB. Associations with gene expression with P-values <1.0 × 10–4 were considered significant. For variants lacking RegulomeDB or GTEx annotations, historic reference identifiers were retrieved and queried when available.

## RESULTS

In our population-based cohort of 3663 melanoma participants, those with incident MPM were older, had a greater proportion of males and their index melanomas were thinner compared to participants with SPM (Supplementary Material, Table S1). Figure 1 presents a stepwise summary of results across the different stages of the analysis.

We investigated the associations between 215 genetic variants and odds of MPM. Results from the multivariable logistic regression for each individual gene variant and additive inheritance model are shown in the Supplementary Material, Table S2. We found 30 nominally significant variants in 14 CK/CKR genes (p<0.05) with MPM, as shown for the dominant and recessive inheritance models in Table 1. The estimated effect (percent increase or decrease) on odds for MPM ranged from 16 to 44% in the dominant model, and 22 to 80% in the recessive model. The estimated per allele effect ranged from 13 to 40%. Statistical significance was evaluated using a nominal cutoff of p < 0.05. Nine variants in CXCR2, CXCR1, ACKR2, CCR9, CCR3, and CCL8 met this criterion, each demonstrating stronger evidence of association with MPM risk (p < 0.009).

The results from the haplotype analyses are shown in Table 2. Five haplotypes in CXCR2, CCR9, CXCL12, and CCL18 were statistically significantly associated (global p-values ranging from 0.026 to 0.0005) with odds of MPM, and with a stronger effect compared to the individual SNPs. For example, for the CXCL12 haplotype formed with variants rs1804430-rs1065297-rs2839696-rs2522-rs12258838 the per haplotype [A-A-A-A-G] adj-OR is 0.34 (95% CI 0.16,0.72), while the per rs2839696-A allele OR is 0.74 (95% CI 0.57–0.96). There were no significant haplotype blocks on CCL8.

We mined the GTEx project database and found statistically significant associations between CK/CKR variants associated with MPM odds (Tables 1 and 2) and gene expression in skin. Ten SNPs in CCR9, CCR3, CXCR2, and CXCR5 affect the expression of FYCO1, CCR5, PNKD, RP11–378A13.1, RUFY4, CXCR2, and BCL9L in skin (p-values 4.4E-5 to 6.21E-32). Eleven variants in CCR9, CCR3, CXCR2, CXCR5, and CXCL12, affect the expression of FYCO1, CCR5, PNKD, RP11–378A13.1, RUFY4, BCL9L, CXCR2, plus RP11–20J15.3 through 78 SNPs in high LD (r2>0.80 and D’>0.95). The nearly significant variant rs7129 (p=0.0507, Table S2) modifies the expression of XCR1 via 13 SNPs in high LD. Detailed information for the tested and proxy SNPs, genes, and associations is shown in the Supplementary Table S4. In line with these findings, Table 3 compiles functional and translational annotations of CK/CKR variants, integrating regulatory evidence linking them to gene expression and potential mechanistic contributions to MPM susceptibility.

## DISCUSSION

In a large cohort of over 3600 incident primary melanoma patients, we evaluated whether inherited variation in chemokine (CK) and chemokine-receptor (CKR) genes are associated with occurrence of subsequent primary melanoma (multiple primary melanoma, MPM). We identified 36 variants in 14 genes associated with MPM through genotypes and haplotypes. Of these, some variants were reported in other large association studies, most are functionally relevant, and several affect the expression of other CK/CKRs and genes involved in apoptosis, autophagy, epithelial-mesenchymal-like transition, macrophages activation, cell invasion, invadopodia, and metastasis in other cancers - directly through the index association variants or through LD-proxy candidate causal SNPs.

The observed associations are biologically plausible given the central role of CK/CKRs as regulators of the tumor microenvironment. Although individual genotypes reached only nominal significance, the findings are supported by multiple lines of evidence: larger effects of haplotypes, published associations, and documented eQTL effects on genes involved in tumorigenic processes relevant to melanoma. These results suggest that inherited CK/CKR variants contribute systemically to the tumor microenvironment. High-risk genotypes/haplotypes may promote a systemic inflammatory state or impair immune surveillance, lowering the threshold for the development of subsequent primary melanoma. To our knowledge, this study is the first to suggest that inherited CK/CKR variants can influence melanoma susceptibility by modulating antitumoral immune responses.

Several chemokine and receptor gene variants have been linked to breast, prostate, colorectal, and other cancers [21–23]. The IL8 [CXCL8]-CXCR1/2 axis has long been recognized as a driver of melanoma progression, particularly in the transition from the radial to vertical growth [24]. In GEM, two significant CXCR1 variants overlap with the seed regions of hsa-mir-335 (rs3092969), hsa-miR-329, hsa-miR-603, and hsa-miR-362–3p (rs2854385) although the relevance of this SNP-miRNA interaction has not been characterized in melanoma. The CXCR2 variant rs4674257*A has been linked to inflammatory cell infiltration and IgA nephropathy progression [25], and a proxy, rs1008562 (R2 0.96) has been associated with increased rectal cancer risk and colorectal cancer-specific mortality [26]. In our data, rs4674257*A, rs1008562*C, and multiple proxies also influence CXCR2 expression in skin (Table S4; p-values 5.69E-06 to 1.43E-09), supporting the GEM findings. CXCR2 regulates mediators such as VEGF, MMP2, MMP9, which are involved in angiogenesis, matrix degradation, and endothelial cell activation [27–28].

CCL18 functions as a pro-tumorigenic, immunosuppressive chemokine in melanoma [29–30] and is implicated in fibrotic processes such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, where higher levels drive fibroblast proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition, and collagen production [31]. In our study, the CCL18 haplotype containing rs2015086*T showed a protective effect, consistent with Wiertz et al. (2020) [31], who reported that the opposite allele (C) is associated with higher CCL18 mRNA in PBMCs and higher serum CCL18. These data support the interpretation that germline variation associated with lower CCL18 activity may reduce susceptibility to developing a subsequent primary melanoma.

The CCL25-CCR9 axis promotes cell migration, proliferation, survival and invasion in several cancers (reviewed in [32]). CCR9 is expressed in melanocytes and melanoma cells, and may influence metastatic tropism to the small intestine, as only melanoma cells isolated from small-bowel metastases respond to it's ligand, CCL25 [32]. A recent large genome-wide association meta-analysis study identified CCL25 among the strongest associations with melanoma susceptibility [33]. Although we did not identify significant CCL25 variants in GEM, we identified several 3’UTR CCR9 variants associated with multiple melanoma risk. Some overlap with seed regions in miRNAs involved in melanoma proliferation and invasion (miR-423p-5p, miR-940, miR382), or suppression (hsa-miR-486–3p). Rs7652331*T, which increased melanoma risk in GEM, has been also linked to prostate cancer progression [34]. In addition, we identified CCR9 proxies that influenced XCR1 expression in skin.

CCL8 promotes melanoma cell growth, invasion, and metastasis [35], and high CCL8 levels correlate with worse outcomes [6], [36]. The intronic CCL8 rs3138037 (T>C or A>G), significantly associated with MPM in GEM, lies in an active regulatory region, with evidence of transcription factor binding and altered chromatin accessibility. A tightly linked SNP, rs3138036 (D’=1.0, R2 =0.99; rs3138037- rs3138036; T=A, C=G), has been associated with lower circulating CCL8 levels [37] but shows no regulatory activity. Given the strong LD, reduced melanoma risk in GEM and lower blood CCL8 levels are most plausibly attributable to rs3138037. CCL8 signals through CCR3 and CCR5. One MPM-associated CCR3 SNP is functional and is in high LD with rs4987053, previously linked to ovarian cancer risk [38], with matched risk alleles. This SNP and several proxies also affect CCR5 expression in sun-exposed skin. The CCR5 rs333 ‘delta 32’ variant, which abolishes CCR5 expression, has been associated with poor prognosis in melanoma patients treated with immunotherapy [8] but neither GEM nor a prior small study [39] found an association with melanoma risk, suggesting context-specific effects, rather than a generalized susceptibility.

The widely studied intronic CXCL12 rs1801157*A, implicated in several hematologic and solid cancers [40], [21], did not independently increase MPM in GEM (OR 1.15, p=0.071). However, this SNP and three highly linked variants (D’1: rs2839696, rs2839695, rs2839689) formed two CXCL12 haplotypes that modified melanoma risk in our study. Rs2839696 overlaps with the miR 635 seed region; rs2839695 overlaps with miR 577; and rs2839689 affects miRNA binding to lncRNA H19, which is dysregulated in multiple tumors, including melanoma [41].

ACKR2 [previously known as D6 and CCBP2] is a scavenger receptor that degrades chemokines, limits tumor growth, immune cell infiltration, angiogenesis, and cancer cell invasion. In contrast, reduced ACKR2 expression promotes proinflammatory chemokines, increased tumor-associated macrophages, and enhanced tumor progression across cancer models. In our study, the functional rs2228467 (V41A, A>G) is inversely associated with MPM risk and has been linked to distinct blood and cerebrospinal fluid profiles [10], [42]. This variant is in strong linkage disequilibrium (D′ = 1) with rs2228468, which synergizes with DARC rs12075 to modulate ACKR2’s sequestration of CCL2 and CCL5, and tumor invasiveness [43–44].

GTEx analyses showed that many of the CK/CKR variants associated with MPM risk and their LD-proxies influence the expression of CKRs (CXCR2, CCR5, XCR1) and of other genes involved in tumorigenesis. For example, melanoma risk CXCR2 alleles in GEM were very strongly linked to higher expression of PNKD in both sun-exposed and unexposed ‘normal’ skin (p-value 4.08E-06 to 3.35E-20). PNKD (MR-1) is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes, melanocytes, and in some immune cells; studies have linked its overexpression to non-small cell lung cancer cells invasiveness in vitro and in vivo [45], colorectal cancer risk [46], an unfavorable prognosis in renal cancer [47]. We also observed risk alleles linked to increased BCL9L expression, a molecule that promotes tumorigenicity through immune-dependent and independent mechanisms in triple-negative breast cancer [48]. In melanoma, BCL9L promotes epithelial-to-mesenchymal-like transition events [49]. Other downstream targets included FYCO1, an autophagy adaptor that promotes cellular migration, invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and invadopodia in vitro [50] and was reported to be differentially expressed in ovarian cancer [51], RUFY4, a paralog of FYCO1 that regulates macroautophagy in primary dendritic cells [52], and RP11–378A13.1, a long non coding RNA differentially expressed in lung adenocarcinoma [53]. Another lnc RNA target, RP1120J15.3, was associated with outcomes in patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma [54]. Evidently, many of the CK/CKR variants identified in our study are interlinked with multiple tumorigenic processes, highlighting the biological plausibility of our findings.

A limitation of this study is the absence of an independent comparable cohort for validation. It is noteworthy that CK/CKR variants did not reach significance in the GWAS meta-analysis reported by Landi et al. (2020) for first primary melanoma [55]. The stringent significance thresholds applied in large GWAS meta-analyses may limit the detection of variants with modest effect sizes, particularly those acting through immune regulatory mechanisms. Among variants previously examined, only CCR3 rs13326331 showed a directionally consistent association, although the estimated effect was minute and did not reach statistical significance (OR, 1.03, 95% CI, 0.9967–1.057). Strengths include the comprehensive assessment of CK/CKR SNPs, a priori selected mostly for their functional relevance and reported associations, the large cohort of incident primary melanomas, and the availability of data on known melanoma risk confounders. Variants were designated as candidate causal variants when they were in very high LD with the index SNPs and supported by regulatory annotation and skin-specific eQTL evidence; nevertheless, these inferences remain probabilistic and do not imply proof of causality in the absence of fine-mapping or further validation. Although none of the associations met a strict threshold corrected for multiple testing (p<0.00023) the proportion of significant variants (16.7%), largely concentrated within chromosomal regions 3p21.31–3p22.3, 2q35, and 10q11.21, is unlikely to be due to chance alone, supporting a true underlying association between CK/CKR loci and multiple primary melanoma risk.

In conclusion, our findings suggest that inherited variation in chemokine and chemokine-receptor genes contributes to the risk of developing subsequent primary melanoma by modulating systemic and local immune responses within the tumor microenvironment. Despite modest effect sizes at the single-variant level, the convergence of haplotype signals, biological and eQTL effects, and prior cancer associations underscores a physiologically coherent role for CK/CKR pathways in melanoma susceptibility. These results highlight immune regulatory mechanisms as determinants of multiple primary melanoma risk and motivate further validation. Future studies will evaluate the effect of CK/CKR variants in relation to tumor characteristics and survival.

# Abstract I

mproving electric vehicles’ range can be achieved by integrating infrared heating panels (IRPs) into the existing Heating Ventilation and Air-Conditioning system to reduce battery energy consumption while maintaining thermal comfort. Localized comfort control enabled by IRPs is facilitated by thermal comfort index feedback to the control strategy, such as the well-known Predicted Mean Vote (PMV). PMV is obtained by solving nonlinear equations iteratively, which is computationally expensive for vehicle control units and may not be feasible for realtime control. This paper presents the design of real-time capable thermal comfort observer based on feedforward artificial neural network (ANN), utilized for estimating the local PMV extended with IRP radiative heating effects. The vehicle under consideration is equipped with 12 heating panels (zones) organized into six controller clusters that rely on the average PMV feedback from its respective zone provided by a dedicated ANN. Each of six ANNs is

designed with five inputs and features an input layer, one fully connected layer and output layer to predict the average cluster PMV. Four inputs—cabin air temperature and relative humidity, cabin inlet air temperature and blower fan flow rate—are shared across all ANNs, while the fifth input is specific to each ANN, representing the clusters’ IRPs average temperature. The training data for ANNs is generated using an experimentally parametrized high-fidelity cabin model which incorporates 12 local IRP zones and CFD-based air distribution model. Bayesian optimization is employed to optimize the ANN structure and training hyperparameters such as number of neurons and learning rate. Performance of ANN observer integrated within overall control strategy is demonstrated in simulation and benchmarked against ideal PMV feedback. Experimental validation through Hardware-in-the-Loop testing demonstrated that the ANNs require less than 3% of the production VCU's processing power while operating at a 100 Hz sampling rate with low memory footprint.

## Introduction E

lectric vehicles are becoming increasingly prevalent in the passenger car market [1], with their popularity expected to continue rising, in part due to incentives aimed at reducing harmful emissions [2]. While the declared range of currently available battery electric vehicles (BEVs) has risen to between 300 km and 500 km, these figures are often significantly reduced in cold conditions, primarily due to the increased energy demand of heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The energy consumption of HVAC system is significantly influenced by environmental conditions and the driver's preferences for thermal comfort. This is confirmed in [3], where laboratory tests on homologation

driving cycle showed that at an ambient temperature of -10°C, the BEV range decreases by 59% compared to its nominal range at 23°C. As a result, it is crucial for BEVs to utilize HVAC systems that efficiently manage the limited electrical energy available, especially in extremely cold conditions. To address this challenge, new energy-efficient HVAC concepts are being explored. These include systems that utilize multiple energy flows, integrate heating and cooling of the passenger compartment, drivetrain, and battery [4, 5], and employ improved technologies such as heat pumps [6], as well as localized heating and cooling methods, such as infrared heating panels (IRP) [7]. Additionally, by separately regulating the air temperature in specific cabin zones, these systems could improve

In parallel, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are increasingly being applied to thermal systems control for various purposes. For example, [12] uses offline trained NARX-RNN model for nonlinear model predictive control design, where ANN approximates the HVAC system dynamics and outputs. Combining localized heating, specifically using IRPs to control the thermal comfort of cabin occupants is demonstrated in [20] Therein, IRP control is based on Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) feedback. Since this strategy relies on PMV feedback, which is not directly measurable but needs to be estimated/observed, a PMV observer needs to be designed. This paper introduces a feedforward artificial neural network (ANN) to estimate the local PMV index in an electric vehicle cabin, accounting for both air distribution and the effects of IRPs in addition to standard PMV calculation. ## Thermal Comfort Index

Thermal comfort indices are used for objective evaluation of thermal comfort in a vehicle cabin [21]. The most widely used index for global thermal comfort is the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) index [18]. However, in a vehicle cabin, the temperature is not necessarily evenly distributed, and in such cases, local thermal comfort indices are applied. One method for determining local thermal comfort is the equivalent temperature method [22], which defines the range of comfortable temperatures for specific body parts in both winter and summer environmental conditions. Other possible methods for determining thermal comfort include the global Dynamic Thermal Sensation model [23], and the more precise, local, Zhang’s thermal comfort model [24]. However, these methods require the use of multi-zone cabin models in simulations, complex calculations of thermophysiological human states such as skin temperature, and are therefore more suitable for applications in 3D computational fluid dynamics simulations. Since the focus of this work is on control systems and a single-zone cabin model is used, the PMV thermal comfort index will be  applied for assessing thermal comfort. In principle, the PMV index can also be applied to determine local thermal comfort by using a simplified calculation of local air temperature and airflow velocity. The PMV index predicts the subjective perception of thermal comfort for a group of people in a given space, expressed as a numerical value, as shown in Table 1. A positive PMV value indicates an environment that is too warm, while a negative value indicates an environment that is too cold. A PMV of zero represents ideal thermal comfort, and according to the standard, the thermally comfortable range is defined as |PMV| < 0.5 [18]. ## Electric Vehicle Cabin Heating System Functional Description

The considered vehicle is equipped with advanced heat pump-based heating system and infrared heating panels placed throughout the cabin. The integrated HVAC system is designed to efficiently manage the heating and cooling of the battery electric vehicle (BEV) passenger compartment, utilizing a R290 refrigerant-based cycle and multiple heat exchange loops, as illustrated in Figure 1. The core of the system is a refrigeration cycle (green) that exchanges heat with two secondary coolant (water-glycol mixture) loops (red and blue). The secondary loops act as intermediaries between the refrigeration cycle and multiple air-to-water heat exchangers (depicted by colored arrows). By redirecting the coolant between heat exchangers, the system can switch between different operating modes. Additionally, a third coolant loop (orange) is dedicated to cooling the vehicle's motor and power electronics. This HVAC system supports a total of seven operating modes, and the details of the system development and its operating modes are provided in [6, 25]. For the purposes of this study, however, the focus is specifically on the heat pump-based heating mode (without waste heat reuse) under the assumption that the powertrain is starting in cold conditions.

Special attention is given to the role of infrared heating panels during the initial heat-up phase, as they significantly enhance passenger comfort during transient conditions. The cabin of the target vehicle is equipped with 16 IRPs located on the doors, roof, visors, and above the driver and passenger's feet, as shown in Figure 2 [25, 26, 36]. These panels provide additional radiant heating, which allows for reducing the load on the HVAC system and improving passenger's thermal comfort [20]. Moreover, IRPs enable localized heating for passengers through the separate control of individual panel groups - clusters. This capability is particularly important in the target vehicle, as localized air conditioning cannot be achieved via airflow due to non-adjustable flaps and air distribution nozzles.

## High-Fidelity Vehicle Cabin Model

A detailed, high-fidelity physics-based simulation model of the HVAC system was implemented in the Dymola simulation environment [27]. The TIL Suite model library [28] is utilized, which includes detailed models of HVAC system components such as compressors, pumps, and heat exchangers, as well as thermodynamic properties of refrigerants, secondary fluids, and moist air. The simulation model has been parameterized based on available design data, experimental data obtained from measurements of individual components and the overall test system [29]. By connecting all the components of the model, a system of differential algebraic equations is obtained and solved using the standard Dymola DASSL integration method. ## Heating System Control Strategy

*Figure 5 shows the block diagram of hierarchical HVAC control strategy based on [20]. It comprises a fixed-gain proportional-integral (PI) cabin air temperature controller, which sets the heating power demand Q˙hR. The heating power demand is achieved at given cabin air temperature Tc and relative humidity φc by the optimal control allocation, which sets the cabin inlet air temperature reference and mass flow, TinR and ṁbf, respectively. The former is achieved by low-level gain-scheduled PI controller that sets the compressor speed reference ncomR (speed control is implemented within e-compressor) while the latter is converted to blower fan voltage Vbf via identified blower fan characteristic. Additional gain-scheduled PI controller ensures that superheat temperature reference ΔTSHR is maintained by commanding EXV position av. Finally, pump speeds np2 and np3 and main radiator fan power level P¯rf are allocated with respect to compressor speed ncom, as it has been showed in [31] that this facilitates the HVAC*

system response and simplifies the strategy design at the expense of minorly increased energy consumption. Note that this control system architecture decouples the cabin control inputs (TinR and ṁbf) and low-level HVAC control, which allows for application of different superimposed cabin air temperature controllers, such as model predictive control to the same HVAC system [32]. It has been shown in [20] that heating panels control can be decoupled from convection heat pump-based system to allow for localized thermal comfort control without affecting the heat pump system. The heating panels control input uIRP is determined by thermal comfort controller that regulates the PMV thermal comfort index of corresponding zone. This structure of panel control allows for localized heating, as each cluster feedback can be based on local PMV feedback. ## Network Architecture

In this study, a feedforward ANN is selected to model the static regression of PMV value. The choice of a

feedforward network is driven by the fact that the PMV value can be accurately predicted using a fixed set of input variables without requiring sequential or temporal dependencies, which makes recurrent networks unnecessary. Feedforward ANNs are also computationally simpler, which is a key advantage when targeting real-time applications in automotive systems. Given their relatively lower number of parameters and simpler training process compared to other network architectures, they are highly suitable for implementation on automotive ECUs where memory and computational resources are limited. Since there is no thermal coupling between the six infrared heating panel clusters, six separate feedforward ANNs are designed, one for each IRP cluster. Each ANN comprises of three layers as depicted in Figure 6. First is the input layer that accepts a set of five input variables. All six ANNs share four input variables that are related to cabin air and cabin inlet air properties since a single zone air heating is employed and these are cabin air temperature Tc, relative humidity φc, inlet air temperature Tin, blower fan flow rate ṁbf. The fifth input of each ANN is the average temperature of cluster’s panels, which is for example of driver’s upper body (cluster 1) defined as

( ) 1 , , , , / 2 IRP IRP DR H IRP DR C T T T = +

This input reflects the cluster’s radiative heating output and is crucial for calculating the cluster’s radiative heating output and is crucial for calculating the local PMV value. Second layer is the single fully-connected hidden layer with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function. ReLU

is chosen for its computational efficiency and ability to introduce non-linearity, which allows the network to model complex relationships between input variables and the resulting PMV value. The number of neurons in the hidden layer is optimized based on the model’s performance, balancing accuracy with computational cost. The final, third layer is the output layer produces the predicted PMV value for the respective panel cluster (see equations (1)-(6)). A linear activation function is applied in this layer, as the output is continuous and directly represents the PMV index, which is a scalar value ranging from -6 to +3. While the proposed design employs six independent ANNs, each responsible for a specific panel cluster, alternative configurations are possible. For instance, a single ANN could be designed to take all relevant inputs from the cabin and panel clusters and generate multiple PMV outputs. Two potential configurations could be the: (i) 10 input-6 output network, where four cabin related and six average panel temperatures are used to predict six cluster PMVs or, (ii) 16 input-12 output network, in which four cabin related inputs and 12 panel temperatures, i.e., each modeled zone panel temperature are used to 12 model outputs (PMV of each zone). While these architectures could reduce the total number of networks required, they introduce significant challenges in terms of training complexity. A network that handles all clusters simultaneously would need to be trained across a broader design space to accurately capture the absence of thermal coupling between clusters. Specifically, it would need to learn that variations in one panel’s temperature do not affect the PMV in other zones. Failure to adequately cover all possible input combinations during training could lead to significant extrapolation errors, particularly when the network encounters control settings it was not explicitly trained on. In contrast, the proposed approach of using separate networks for each cluster simplifies the training process. By treating each cluster independently, the training dataset can be generated more efficiently, as all clusters can be set to a common control input during data collection. This reduces the size of the design space and ensures that each network is focused solely on modeling its respective cluster’s behavior, leading to more accurate and reliable PMV predictions.

## Training and Validation Dataset Generation

## Training and Hyperparameter Optimization

The design of the artificial neural network (ANN) training process is structured into two layers: an outer optimization layer and an inner training layer. This two-layer approach ensures both optimal network architecture and

efficient training, leading to improved accuracy in predicting the PMV values. In the outer layer, Bayesian optimization is employed to automatically determine the hyperparameters of the network [33]. The key hyperparameters optimized via Bayesian optimization include the number of neurons in hidden layers and training parameters to improve the training accuracy, whereas the inner layer trains the individual network, i.e., determines the neuron weights and biases for given number of neurons and training parameter set. The optimization of the hidden layer size in each network is critical for achieving a balance between prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. A network that is too large may overfit the training data and require excessive computational resources, whereas a too small network may fail to capture the complexity of the thermal interactions in the cabin, leading to poor performance in predicting thermal comfort. The objective function of Bayesian optimization is the minimization of root mean square error (RMSE) of predicted PMV values with respect to actual PMV value, through a limited number of objective evaluations and with a maximum run-time (set to one hour herein). The constraints on the hyperparameters to be optimized are set as follows:

The Bayesian optimization is repeated separately for all six neural networks, ensuring tailored hyperparameters for each panel cluster's ANN. The inner layer involves the actual training of the ANNs once the hyperparameters are selected by the Bayesian optimization process. The inner layer for ANN training is based on Matlab’s Deep Learning Toolbox, specifically employing the trainnet function with the goal of minimizing the mean squared error between predicted and actual PMV values. The chosen optimizer for training is the stochastic gradient-based method Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) [34]. ADAM is chosen due to its ability to adjust learning rates dynamically and its robust performance in minimizing error across diverse training conditions. The maximum number of epochs used for training is set to 500 and data is shuffled with each epoch, while the mini-batch size is optimized via Bayesian optimization. The learning rate follows a piecewise schedule, with the initial rate set via Bayesian

For the given parameters, Bayesian optimization problem and inputs, the training takes around 10 minutes per network on average, while the Bayesian optimization is time constrained to one hour per network. Note that the ANN training time will highly depend on the machine on which it has been performed as well as network architecture and parameters. Since the training procedure is relatively fast, it allows for retraining in case of hardware changes (e.g., IRP positioning) and evaluation of various network architectures quickly in the virtual environment. ## Validation Results

The optimal hyperparameters and the validation results in terms of root-mean square error for each neural network are summarized in Table 3. The results indicate that all ANNs perform consistently well across the training, test and validation datasets with only minor variations. The highest RMSE is around 0.065 for ANN3, while the lowest RMSE is approximately 0.0310 for ANN2. Considering that the ideal comfort is defined as PMV being in comfortable range of |PMV| < 0.5, the RMSE indicates that the prediction capability of ANNs is sufficiently accurate even with a relatively simple architecture. While ANN2 and ANN4 have relatively large architectures with 82 and 79 neurons, respectively, most of the networks operate effectively with fewer than 20 neurons (e.g., ANN1 and ANN6 have 18 and 14 neurons). This indicates that even simple architectures can yield highly accurate PMV predictions. Figure 8 shows a snapshot comparison between the target PMV output (original dataset value) and ANN-predicted PMV output for one example of testing dataset (a) and training dataset (b). These results indicate that trained ANN predicts the PMV values well with only minor deviations.

## Real-Time Implementation on Vehicle Electronic Control Unit

In order to test the real-time feasibility of designed observer, the ANN PMV observers are implemented in the production electronic control unit Rimac Technology ECU101 [35]. The ECU is built around NXP automotive PowerPC MPC5744P CPU microprocessor unit featuring two 32-bit cores with a clock frequency of 200 MHz, internal RAM of 384 kB and flash memory of 2500 kB. The ECU is programmed in Matlab/Simulink and the C-code is automatically generated and built. The code generation of neural networks is supported with MATLAB Coder Interface for Deep Learning Libraries. The ECU code includes service layer, communication layer (CAN/LIN and analog/digital inputs/outputs), hardware abstraction layer and application software layer. The task scheduling is managed by splitting the code into 100 tasks with 100 microseconds duration per task, resulting in 10 ms sampling time. All six ANN observers have been integrated within the overall HVAC control strategy. The whole strategy with observer has been implemented as per block diagram shown in Figure 5 in Matlab/Simulink environment in the application software layer. The ANNs are integrated in the scheduling framework and assigned with a maximum of three tasks, effectively being allocated a maximum of 3% of ECU’s processing capacity. The ECU is tested in processor-in-the-loop approach by connecting it via CAN with Speedgoat Mobile M3 unit to feed the inputs as illustrated in Figure 11. Desktop computer controls the Speedgoat through Matlab/ Simulink and it is connected via XCP over CAN to the ECU

## Summary/Conclusions

In conclusion, the artificial neural networks (ANNs) designed for real-time implementation on automotive

electronic control units (ECUs) have been successfully applied to the estimation of the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) for thermal comfort control. The network design process, which utilized Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning, resulted in highly efficient ANNs. These networks accurately predict the PMV thermal comfort index with root-mean-square error (RMSE) values ranging between 0.0310 and 0.0658 across various network configurations, ensuring reliable PMV predictions within the thermal comfort range of |PMV|< 0.5. The ANNs were integrated into a comprehensive HVAC control strategy, with their effectiveness demonstrated through simulations in a nonlinear environment and further validated in real-time by deploying them on production-grade ECUs. Simulation results confirmed the ANNs' effectiveness in real-world thermal comfort control scenarios with marginal performance. Specifically, using the ANN-predicted PMV in the thermal comfort control had an impact in the direction of increased energy consumption and improved thermal comfort, primarily caused by the air temperature sensor dynamics delaying the inputs for the observer. Processor-in-theloop testing demonstrated that the designed networks can operate within the 10 ms sampling period required for real-time control. The ANN observers perform within 200 microseconds of processing time, consuming less than 3% of the ECU's resources. These results confirm that the ANN-based observers are capable of meeting stringent automotive performance requirements, including computational efficiency and real-time responsiveness. Future efforts should be directed to optimizing the architecture of neural network in terms of testing the network with additional layer and potentially reducing the number of neurons as well as testing various activation functions in the hidden layer to find the optimal compromise in terms of computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. Similarly, Bayesian optimization layer could be converted into multi-objective problem to directly trade-off accuracy (current cost) and network complexity (number of neurons). This study has focused on a single vehicle with a specific heat pump and HVAC architecture. Future work should evaluate the scalability of the proposed solution across different vehicle platforms and HVAC configurations, including the retraining efforts in case of various panel configurations. Testing across a broader range of vehicles, climates, and driving conditions will be crucial to ensure robustness and generalizability. Moreover, while this paper primarily focused on using ANN-based PMV observers to provide feedback for controlling infrared heating panels, the potential applications extend beyond this target. The PMV observer can be used for diagnostics purposes to provide insight into system performance and identify any thermal comfort issues in real-time, human-machine interface in terms of offering the passengers direct feedback on thermal comfort levels and enhance user experience, and finally serve as reduced-order prediction model in the model predictive control.
